frames.narration: A customer asks "refund for a damaged parcel". The index holds 10 million chunks as 768-dimension vectors. The question must be turned into a vector first.
The same model that embedded the articles returns a 768-float vector (3 KB). Close vectors mean similar meaning; nothing else about the text is kept.
Brute force would compare the query with all 10M vectors: about 30 GB read and 10M distance computations per query. Too slow, so the index must skip almost all of them.
IVF first compares the query with the 4,096 cell centroids and picks the 8 nearest (nprobe = 8). Only those 8 lists, about 19,500 vectors, will be scanned.

The index scans compressed 96-byte codes of those 19,500 vectors, skipping any that are not tenant 42. Codes hold the whole collection in about 1 GB instead of 30 GB, but their distances are approximate.
The 100 best candidates are re-ranked with their full float32 vectors from SSD. Only 100 reads, and the final order is exact among them.
The top 10 chunks go back to the client after at most about 24,000 distance computations instead of 10 million, around 400 times fewer, in a few milliseconds.

Measured against brute force on 1,000 sample queries, this setting returns on average about 94 percent of the true top 10 (recall@10). Raising nprobe to 32 raises recall and latency; lowering it does the opposite. Tune on your own data.
